sections.title: Situation
sections.prompt: What was the setting, what was your role, and why did you have no authority over the people who had to change?
criteria: Names the company type, their own role and one number for scale (revenue, volume or headcount) in three sentences or fewer
States plainly that the other org did not report to them or their manager
Quantifies the problem in money or volume a year, with the arithmetic shown
Names a deadline or planning window that made the timing matter

sections.title: Stakeholders
sections.prompt: Who had to change, what did each of them want, and how did you bring them along?
criteria: Names the decision-maker in the other org and what they were protecting (a date, a budget or a commitment)
Includes at least one person below the decision-maker they won over first
Includes their own manager or director and what that person gave up
Ends with one idea that ties the stakeholders together

sections.title: Options
sections.prompt: What routes did you consider for getting the change, and why did most of them fail?
criteria: Lists escalation as an option and says why they did not use it
Lists doing it themselves (a workaround in their own system) and names its long-term cost
Lists waiting for the next planning cycle and prices the delay
Compares the options on the same criteria, such as time to effect and who owns the result

sections.title: Decision and Trade-offs
sections.prompt: What did you decide to ask for, and what did you give up to get it?
criteria: Names one specific ask, sized in people and time, not 'alignment'
Names something they or their team gave up (roadmap, headcount or credit)
Says how the ask was made easy to stop, with a checkpoint and a condition
Uses 'I' for the decision and the trade, not 'we'

sections.title: Economics
sections.prompt: What was at stake in numbers, and what did the change cost?
criteria: Derives the annual value at stake from volume and unit cost
Counts the cost of their own give-up (delayed launch or lent engineers), not only the other org's
Separates new spend from people already on payroll
Labels every assumed figure as assumed

sections.title: Org and Ownership
sections.prompt: Who owned the work during the change and after it?
criteria: Leaves the other org owning the result after a dated handover
Describes their own role during the work, such as tech lead with no reporting line
Names a written agreement, such as a data contract or an OKR, that outlasts the people involved

sections.title: Plan and Milestones
sections.prompt: What did you do in what order, before and after the other org agreed?
criteria: Shows the influence steps before the decision meeting (evidence, one-to-ones, a pilot)
Says who saw the proposal before the decision-maker did, and why
Has at least one checkpoint with a measurable condition during the work
Gives a timeline in weeks or months

sections.title: Risk and Governance
sections.prompt: What could have gone wrong, for the other org, the customer and the relationship?
criteria: Names the risk to the other org's commitment and how it was protected
Names a risk to customers from the change itself and a control for it
Names a relationship risk, such as the decision-maker feeling ambushed, and how it was avoided
Quantifies at least one risk

sections.title: Metrics
sections.prompt: What was the measured result, and what showed nothing else broke?
criteria: Gives a quantified result with a before and after number
Pairs the result with a guard metric, such as the other org's date being hit
Includes a result that matters to the other org, not only to them
Claims the measured result, not the full theoretical value

sections.title: Communication
sections.prompt: How did you tell each audience, and how do you tell the story in two minutes?
criteria: Tells the story in STAR order (Situation, Task, Action, Result) in about two minutes
Gives each key audience a different one-line message
Says what they would do differently, specifically
Keeps the Action part the longest, in first person
